costGuide.title: Mercedes-Benz M104 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting an M104 engine typically takes 10-14 hours at £65-£85/hr (independent) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for this engine is the condition of the cylinder head gasket, the front main seal, and whether the infamous biodegradable engine wiring harness (on 1993-1995 models) has been upgraded to a modern PTFE loom. Because the M104 is a complex 24-valve unit, recon specialists will typically strip the top end to inspect the head for warping, replace all brittle seals, and verify the wiring harness integrity as standard. For a full breakdown of market rates, see our full reconditioned engine cost guide.

failures.title: Mercedes-Benz M104 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Biodegradable Wiring Harness Degradation - 1993-1995 models
items.onset: Age-related (typically fails between 10-15 years of age)
items.whatHappens: Mercedes-Benz used an environmentally friendly, biodegradable insulation on the engine wiring harness (specifically the throttle body and upper harness) for a few years in the mid-90s. Over time, the insulation flakes off, exposing bare copper wires that short out against each other or the engine block. This causes erratic idle, limp mode, blown fuses, and can even damage the ECU.
items.repairVsReplace: The only viable repair is a complete replacement of the wiring harness with a modern, non-biodegradable PTFE loom. Attempting to tape or patch the harness is a temporary fix that will inevitably fail again.

items.title: Head Gasket Failure - All variants, especially 3.0L and 3.2L
items.whatHappens: The M104 is notorious for head gasket failure, typically occurring at the rear of the engine block near the firewall. Symptoms include external coolant leaks dripping onto the bellhousing, coolant loss without visible external leaks, and occasionally oil and coolant mixing.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early before the cylinder head warps, a head gasket replacement and head skim is a standard repair. If the head is severely warped or the block is damaged, a full reconditioned M104 unit is required.

items.title: Oil Leaks (Valve Cover, Oil Filter Housing, Front Main) - All variants
items.whatHappens: The M104 features several gaskets that harden and shrink with age and heat cycles. The most common leak points are the valve cover gaskets (leaking onto the exhaust manifolds and causing a burning oil smell), the oil filter housing gasket, and the front main crankshaft seal.
items.repairVsReplace: These are routine maintenance items. Replacing the gaskets and seals is relatively inexpensive in terms of parts, though the oil filter housing and front main seal require significant labour to access.

failures.goodYearsLine: The M104 is widely regarded as one of the smoothest and most durable inline-6 engines Mercedes ever built. Post-1996 units (which feature the updated non-biodegradable wiring harness) are highly prized, and units maintained with regular oil changes routinely exceed 250,000 miles without major internal bottom-end issues .

variants.title: M104 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: ═══════════════════════════════════════ INTRO: The M104 family shares the same fundamental DOHC inline-6 block architecture, but displacement and engine management (KE-Jetronic vs HFM/LH-Jetronic) vary significantly. Identifying your exact sub-code is mandatory, as fitting the wrong revision can lead to severe mechanical and electrical incompatibility. - Fitted to: E-Class W124 (280E), E-Class W210 (E 280), S-Class W140 (280 SE, S 280) - Key technical difference: The entry-level 2.8L variant, featuring a shorter stroke and HFM engine management. It was designed to meet specific tax-bracket displacement limits in several European markets. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; highly susceptible to the biodegradable wiring harness issue if built between 1993 and 1995. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with 3.2L variants due to different crankshafts, engine mounts, and ECU/fuel mapping. - Fitted to: E-Class W124 (300E-24), SL-Class R129 (300 SL-24) - Key technical difference: The original 24-valve evolution of the M103 block, featuring a 3.0L displacement and early KE-Jetronic mechanical fuel injection with electronic overlay (EZR). - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; the early KE-Jetronic system suffers from the same control plunger corrosion as the M103. - Interchange note: Not interchangeable with later HFM/LH-Jetronic variants without swapping the entire intake manifold, throttle body, wiring harness, and ECU. - Fitted to: S-Class W140 (300 SE 2.8 / 320 SE), G-Class W463 (320 GE) - Key technical difference: A 3.2L variant specifically calibrated for the heavier W140 S-Class and rugged W463 G-Class, featuring revised accessory brackets, heavy-duty engine mounts, and specific LH-Jetronic mapping for low-end torque. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; G-Class variants may experience accelerated front main seal wear due to extreme off-road operating angles. - Interchange note: Requires matching sump, oil pickup, and accessory drives for G-Class applications; passenger car variants are not directly interchangeable with off-road specs without modification. - Fitted to: E-Class W124 (320E), E-Class W210 (E 320), SL-Class R129 (320 SL) - Key technical difference: The volume-seller 3.2L variant for the E-Class and SL lines, featuring the updated HFM engine management system and a revised cylinder head casting for improved high-RPM airflow. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; the HFM throttle body is prone to internal potentiometer wear, causing idle surging. - Interchange note: Shares the core 3.2L architecture with the .960, but the engine mounts, wiring harness routing, and ECU mapping are specific to the W124/W210/R129 chassis.

relatives.description: the older 12-valve inline-6 that the M104 replaced, sharing the same robust SOHC architecture but lacking the refined 24-valve head design and improved high-RPM breathing of the M104 family.

the compact 90-degree V6 that eventually replaced the M104 inline-6 across the E-Class and S-Class range, offering comparable power and torque in a shorter, lighter package with improved emissions compliance.

the contemporary 2.0L-2.3L inline-4 that shared the same transitional era of engine management (moving from KE-Jetronic to HFM/LH-Jetronic) and similar wiring harness vulnerabilities, but in a smaller 4-cylinder configuration.

variants.closing: The engine code is stamped on the right-hand side of the cylinder block, near the oil filter housing. It will also be listed on your V5C logbook under "Engine Capacity" or visible via a VIN decode. Not sure? Enter your registration above for instant confirmation.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement M104 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used M104 engine makes sense only if it comes with verifiable service history and documented proof of a recent head gasket replacement and a modern, non-biodegradable wiring harness upgrade. Given the age of these vehicles and the labour-intensive nature of the rear head gasket leak, buying a used unit with unknown history is a significant financial risk.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned M104 engine is the sweet spot for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will proactively address the common failure points by replacing the head gasket, skimming the cylinder head, fitting a modern PTFE wiring harness, and replacing all brittle valve cover and oil seals, giving the engine a fresh lease on life.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full M104 engine rebuild is highly justified for classic W124 320E or R129 SL restorations where originality, matching numbers, and maximum longevity are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block, new pistons/rings, and a balanced crankshaft.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your M104 engine is installed by specialists familiar with classic Mercedes DOHC and HFM/LH-Jetronic systems, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the M104 is typically found in W124, W210, W140, and W463 vehicles valued between £3,000 and £20,000+ (with low-mileage R129 and late W124 models commanding significantly higher premiums), a full replacement is generally financially viable. However, if the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing .

items.question: What is the most common failure on the M104 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are biodegradable wiring harness degradation (on 1993-1995 models), rear head gasket failure, and oil leaks from the valve cover or front main seal. The wiring harness insulation flakes off and causes electrical shorts, while the head gasket tends to fail at the rear of the block, leading to coolant loss. → Get quotes for a rebuilt M104 with these issues resolved

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the M104 engine?
items.answer: The M104 was fitted to the W124 and W210 E-Class (280E, 300E-24, 320E, E 280, E 320), the W140 S-Class (280 SE, 320 SE), the R129 SL-Class (300 SL-24, 320 SL), and the W463 G-Class (300 GE, 320 GE), serving as the definitive 24-valve inline-6 petrol for these chassis between 1989 and 1999. → Check your registration to confirm your exact M104 fitment

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned M104 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned M104 is strongly recommended over a used unit. A proper rebuild will proactively address the fatal flaws of age by replacing the head gasket, skimming the cylinder head, fitting a modern non-biodegradable PTFE wiring harness, and replacing all brittle seals, whereas a used engine with unknown history risks immediate, labour-intensive electrical or cooling system repairs. → Compare reconditioned M104 engine prices from UK specialists

items.question: What is the difference between M104.940, .950, .960, and .980?
items.answer: The M104.940 is the 2.8L variant, the .950 is the early 3.0L variant with KE-Jetronic fuel injection, the .960 is the 3.2L variant calibrated for the heavier S-Class and G-Class, and the .980 is the volume-seller 3.2L variant for the E-Class and SL-Class featuring updated HFM engine management. They share the same core block, but the engine management, cylinder head casting, and accessory drives differ significantly. → Enter your reg above to identify your exact M104 sub-code ═══════════════════════════════════════
